content: Effective oral hygiene practices performed regularly are essential for maintaining optimal oral health. One-to-one oral hygiene advice (OHA) is often provided in dental settings to motivate individuals and improve their oral health. However, the effectiveness of such interventions and the most efficient methods remain uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of one-to-one OHA, delivered by dental professionals in a clinical setting, on patients' oral health, hygiene practices, behaviors, and attitudes, compared to either no advice or advice delivered in alternative formats. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, up to November 10, 2017. Ongoing trials were also identified through ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date. Reference lists of relevant articles and systematic reviews were manually searched, and authors of eligible trials were contacted to identify unpublished data. The review included randomized controlled trials that assessed the effects of one-to-one OHA provided by dental professionals in a clinical setting, with a minimum follow-up period of 8 weeks. Participants included both healthy individuals and those with well-defined medical conditions. Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were conducted independently by at least two reviewers, with consensus achieved through discussion or the involvement of a third reviewer when necessary. Nineteen studies, involving a total of 4,232 participants, met the inclusion criteria. These studies exhibited significant clinical heterogeneity in terms of interventions, populations, and outcome measures, precluding the pooling of data for meta-analysis. Instead, the data were categorized into comparison groups based on similar interventions. 1. Comparison 1: One-to-one OHA versus no OHA Four studies compared one-to-one OHA with no OHA. Two studies assessed gingivitis outcomes, with one small study showing inconsistent results at 3 and 6 months, while the other provided very low-quality evidence of a benefit for OHA at all time points. For plaque outcomes, low-quality evidence suggested a benefit for OHA in reducing plaque levels at all time points. Two studies evaluated dental caries at 6 and 12 months, respectively, with very low-quality evidence indicating a benefit for OHA at 12 months. 2. Comparison 2: Personalized OHA versus routine OHA Four studies compared personalized OHA with routine OHA. There was minimal evidence to suggest any significant differences in outcomes related to gingivitis, plaque, or dental caries. The quality of evidence was very low. 3. Comparison 3: Self-management versus professional OHA Five trials compared self-management approaches with professional OHA. There was little evidence to indicate differences in outcomes for gingivitis or plaque. None of the studies measured dental caries. The quality of evidence was very low. 4. Comparison 4: Enhanced OHA versus routine OHA Seven trials compared enhanced OHA with routine OHA. There was little evidence to suggest differences in outcomes for gingivitis, plaque, or dental caries. The quality of evidence was very low. The authors concluded that there is insufficient high-quality evidence to recommend any specific one-to-one OHA method as being effective in improving oral health or as being superior to other methods. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are necessary to identify the most effective and efficient one-to-one OHA strategies for maintaining and improving oral health. Future trials should address the limitations identified in the current body of evidence.
